title: How to Pace an Inline Speed Skating Race Without Blowing Up
thumbnail_text: Why you fade after a fast start

scenes.heading: How to Pace an Inline Speed Skating Race
scenes.sub: Set a pace you can hold, then spend it at the end
scenes.chapter: The whole plan in one line
scenes.narration: This guide gives you a simple race plan that stops you blowing up halfway. Decide your target pace before the start gun, rather than letting the pack decide it for you. Then hold the first third a shade easier than target. Sit exactly on target through the middle. And spend whatever is left in the final third. Over the next few minutes you will learn how to set a target you can hold, how to turn it into one lap split, how pacing changes with distance, how to race in a pack, and how to rescue a race you started too hard.

scenes.heading: Early seconds are borrowed, not banked
bullets: 3000m on a 200m track is 15 laps
3 laps, 2 seconds fast: 6 gained
Pay back 3 to 4 a lap for 12 laps
Net loss: 36 to 48 seconds
Technique fades before the legs do
scenes.chapter: Why a fast start costs you
scenes.narration: Work it through on a real race. A 3000 metre race on a 200 metre track is fifteen laps. Go two seconds a lap quicker than target for the first three laps, and you have gained six seconds. Now pay for it over the remaining twelve laps, at a typical three or four seconds a lap. You have lost thirty six to forty eight seconds. When you skate above the effort you can sustain, fatigue builds faster than your body can clear it. Once that starts, you cannot stop it mid race. You can only slow down. There is a second cost too. Your technique collapses before your legs do. You lose depth in the knee bend, the push gets shorter, and you start skating high and choppy, right when efficiency matters most.

scenes.heading: Three shapes a race can take
scenes.narration: This chart shows three ways a race can look. Each bar is your speed across five equal parts of the race. The orange row on top is the fast start. It leads early, and every part after that is slower than the one before. It finishes slowest of all. The blue row in the middle is an even pace. The bars stay the same height all the way to the line. The green row at the bottom is a slightly rising pace. It starts a little easier and gets faster in each part, so the skater is quickest at the finish. The two bottom shapes are what good races look like. The skater who looks composed on the last lap is almost never the one who led the first.

scenes.heading: Find a target pace you can hold
bullets: Use a recent effort, not an old best
Solo time trial, record every lap
Pick the lap you could repeat
Rehearse that lap time in tempo repeats
Check it again every few weeks
scenes.narration: A target pace is useless if it comes from hope. It has to come from something you have already done. The best source is a recent full effort over a similar distance, on a similar surface, in similar weather. Here is how to find a number you can trust. Skate a solo time trial over your race distance, or about half of it for a long race. Make it hard but controlled, and record every lap. Then look for the lap you could have repeated again and again, not the fastest one. That lap is close to your race pace. Rehearse that exact lap time in training with tempo repeats and short recoveries, so your legs learn what it feels like. And check it every few weeks, because your fitness moves.

scenes.heading: Turn it into one lap split
bullets: Divide goal time by the number of laps
3000m in 5 minutes: 20 seconds a lap
10km in 20 minutes: 48 a lap
Round it to read in one glance
Write the number on your hand
scenes.chapter: Turning it into a lap split
scenes.narration: A target time is no use to you at speed. A lap split is. Divide your goal time by the number of laps, and round it to something you can read in one glance. Fifteen laps of a 200 metre track makes a 3000 metre race. A goal of five minutes is three hundred seconds, so that is twenty seconds a lap. A 10 kilometre race on a 400 metre road circuit is twenty five laps. A goal of twenty minutes works out at forty eight seconds a lap. Write the number on your hand or your bottle. In a race you will not do sums. You will only compare. One more thing. Heat raises the cost of the same speed, so on a hot day pace the first third by trained effort and let the clock confirm it.

scenes.heading: Pacing changes with distance
bullets: 300m: everything from the first stride
500m: hard start, then hold your form
1000m: controlled opening, drive the last lap
3000m to 5000m: easy, on target, faster
10000m and marathon: steady, chosen surges
scenes.narration: Pacing is not the same for every event. A 300 metre time trial and a marathon ask opposite things of you in the first ten seconds. In a 300 metre time trial, give everything from the first stride and accept a small fade. The common error is holding back and never reaching top speed. In a 500, start hard, then hold your form rather than chasing more speed. In a 1000, open strong but controlled, stay steady, then drive the last lap. For 3000 and 5000 metres, go a shade easier than target, then on target, then faster. In a 10000 or a points race, hold a steady base pace with surges you choose. In a marathon, open comfortably, settle into a group, and save your effort for late. Leading early because it feels easy is the classic mistake.

scenes.heading: One plan for a distance race
scenes.narration: Here is that plan for a distance race, split into three parts from start to finish. In the first third, skate a shade easier than target. It should feel too easy. That is the point. In the middle third, sit exactly on target. Check one lap time and hold your position. In the final third, spend what is left. Stop managing the race and empty the tank. Look at the warning along the bottom. If the first third already feels hard, the plan has failed. Start easing off now, not at halfway. The same three part plan works from 1000 metres all the way to a marathon. Only the size of the margin between the phases changes.

scenes.heading: Corners and packs change the job
bullets: Uneven splits? Check your corners first
Carry speed through the bend
Sitting in costs less effort than leading
Cover surges that open real gaps
Barely holding on? Skate your own pace
scenes.narration: A bad corner can cost you as much as a mispaced first lap, only more quietly. If your splits swing by a second or more while your effort stays even, look at your corners before your fitness. Carry speed into the bend and hold your line. Otherwise an even effort turns into a series of small sprints down every straight. Pack racing is a different problem. You no longer control your own speed, so your job becomes choosing which surges to follow. Sitting in a group costs noticeably less effort than leading it. A surge that opens a real gap has to be covered. A skater who attacks every few laps and always comes back does not. And if you are only just hanging on at the back while the pace is steady, drop out and skate your own pace. You will almost always get a better time.

scenes.heading: Already gone out too fast?
bullets: Back off gradually, never stop dead
Go back to your technique checklist
Let go of the original target
Find a slightly slower group and sit in
Write down your splits afterwards
scenes.narration: It happens to everybody. The race is not over, but the next lap or two decide how bad it gets. First, back off gradually instead of stopping the effort dead. Next, switch from your lap time to your technique. Get the knee bend back, lengthen the push, and let the recovery leg relax. Form is what you can still control. Then let go of the original target. Chasing a time that is already gone turns a slightly disappointing race into a very bad one. Find a group going a little slower than you were, and sit in. Recovering behind someone is far easier than recovering alone. And afterwards, write your lap splits down. A badly paced race is excellent data if you actually look at it.

scenes.heading: Your gear and your body
bullets: Race on the platform you trained on
Wheel size changes your stride count per lap
Chest pain or dizziness: stop, see a doctor
Lasting pain, swelling or numbness: get checked
scenes.narration: Pacing is a skill, not a purchase, with one exception. Race on the frame and wheel platform you did your pace work on. Wheel size changes how far each stride carries you, and so your stride count per lap. That is the rhythm your legs have memorised, so do not change it in race week. Now, your body. Heavy breathing, burning legs and a thumping heart are normal in a hard race. Chest pain or pressure, dizziness, feeling faint, or an unusually irregular heartbeat are not. Neither are symptoms that do not settle once you stop. Those are reasons to stop the race and get checked by a doctor. The same goes for pain that lasts more than a few days, or any swelling or numbness.

scenes.heading: Choose your surges. Hold back early. Spend it late.
scenes.sub: Full guide at livelica.com, link in the description
scenes.narration: If you remember one thing, make it this. Decide your pace before the gun, keep the first third a shade easy, and spend what is left at the end. In a pack, choose which surges you follow instead of answering all of them. And if you go out too fast, back off gradually and rebuild your technique, rather than chasing a time that has already gone. Pace a race well three or four times, and you will stop needing the plan written down. The full guide, with answers on heats and new tracks, is on the LiveLica blog. The link is in the description.
